correctness.rationale: The symmetry assumption forces one fixed vertex and two reflected vertex pairs; side-one geometry gives x∈[1/4,1], y=sqrt(1-(x-1/2)^2), u=sqrt(1-x^2), z=y+u. All ten distances sum to 5+2sqrt(z^2+1/4)+2x+2sqrt(1+2x); checking the five edge-normal support widths reduces min width to three explicit candidates. The proof partitions [1/4,1] into bounded subintervals and handles the final strict ratio monotonicity, not a finite sample. Independently reconstructed all ten pairwise distances and every edge-normal width for 40,001 samples, attaining 4+6sqrt(3) only at x=1 on that grid; this corroborates but does not prove continuum extremality. x=1 is weakly convex and the strict convex family has supremum only, exactly as claimed.

originality.rationale: Audet–Ninin 2013 full journal manuscript, section 4, states total vertex-pair distance optimization at odd n as Conjecture 9 with numerical n=5,7,9 evidence, not a proof; their perimeter/diameter/area theorems do not prove it. Dumitrescu 2013 Theorems 2 and 5 optimize pairwise distances for prescribed perimeter without equilateral and minimal-width normalization, so neither exact ratio nor symmetric equality follows. Direct primary and published-result searches found no stronger proof of this reflection-symmetric n=5 case. The restriction matches the conjectured trapezoidal extremal shape rather than an arbitrary manufactured slice; older unindexed geometric inequalities remain priority risk.
residual_risks: The unrestricted Audet–Ninin odd equilateral conjecture is NOT claimed solved; reflection symmetry restriction is essential.
An older unindexed special symmetric-pentagon inequality might encode the constant.
Strict convex case has supremum not attained: weak trapezoid is a boundary degeneracy.
